content.heading: What a Portfolio Is For
content.body:
A pile is not a portfolio

Most first accounts are piles. You bought a stock a friend mentioned, then a fund your employer offered, then something that was going up, then a few shares of a company whose products you use. Each purchase made sense on its own. Together they answer no question, because none was asked.

A portfolio starts from the other end. You state what the money is for, when you need it, and how much of it you can afford to see disappear temporarily along the way. Then every position has to justify its place against those three constraints. If it cannot, it is not in the portfolio, however good the story.

That is the whole difference. Not the number of holdings, not whether you own funds or single names, not whether it is up this year. A portfolio is a set of holdings that was designed backwards from a goal. A pile is a set of holdings that was accumulated forwards from impulses.

This lesson gives you the three inputs, shows you how to turn a goal into a required return, and explains why the horizon, not the return, decides how much risk you may take.

The three inputs

Goal. A goal is an amount and a date. "Retire comfortably" is a wish. "$60,000 by September 2036" is a goal. The amount lets you compute what return you need; the date tells you how long the money has to get there and how long it has to recover if something goes wrong.

Horizon. Horizon is the time between today and the date you start spending the money. It is the most important number in the whole exercise, because it determines whether a large fall is a temporary inconvenience or a permanent loss. Money that will be spent in two years cannot absorb a 40% fall. Money that will be spent in twenty years can, provided you do not sell at the bottom.

Risk budget. Risk budget is the largest temporary fall you can accept without abandoning the plan. Write it as a percentage and as a dollar figure, because they feel different. "25%" sounds tolerable in the abstract; "$15,000 of my $60,000 gone by Christmas" is what it looks like when it happens. If the dollar figure would make you sell, the percentage is too high.

Most people set the third number too high because they set it in a calm market. Set it as if you were already in the drawdown.

Required return versus available return

Once you have an amount, a date and a starting balance, the goal implies a required rate of return. The market, meanwhile, offers whatever it offers. Your job is to see whether the two are compatible.

If the required return is low, you have room to take less risk than the market maximum, and you should consider doing so, because a lower-risk portfolio is one you are more likely to hold through a bad year. If the required return is higher than anything a sensible portfolio has delivered over long periods, the goal itself is wrong: you need to save more, extend the date, or reduce the amount. Taking more risk to close the gap is the one option that does not work reliably, because higher expected return comes bundled with a wider range of outcomes, including the outcome where you miss by more.

The long-run reference points, from Aswath Damodaran's compilation of annual returns 1928 to 2023, are roughly 9.8% a year compounded for the S&P 500 including dividends, about 4.9% for 10-year Treasury bonds and about 3.3% for 3-month Treasury bills, all before inflation and before costs. These are 96-year averages that contain a Depression, a war, a decade of double-digit inflation and three 50% crashes. They tell you what a very patient investor got, not what the next decade will pay.

Worked example

Goal: $60,000 in 10 years for a house deposit. Starting balance $15,000. You can add $3,000 at the end of each year. What return does the plan require?

Future value of the starting balance plus the contributions:

FV = 15,000 × (1 + r)^10 + 3,000 × [((1 + r)^10 − 1) ÷ r]

Try r = 4%:

  • (1.04)^10 = 1.4802
  • Starting balance: 15,000 × 1.4802 = $22,203
  • Contributions: 3,000 × [(1.4802 − 1) ÷ 0.04] = 3,000 × 12.006 = $36,018
  • Total: $58,221. Short by about $1,800.

Try r = 5%:

  • (1.05)^10 = 1.6289
  • Starting balance: 15,000 × 1.6289 = $24,433
  • Contributions: 3,000 × [(1.6289 − 1) ÷ 0.05] = 3,000 × 12.578 = $37,734
  • Total: $62,167. Over by about $2,200.

The target sits between the two, at roughly 4.5% a year.

Now compare with the reference points. A 4.5% requirement is below the historical bond return and far below the stock return. The goal does not force you into an all-stock portfolio. A mix that historically returned 6% or so with much smaller falls than stocks alone would have got you there with margin. That margin is worth having, because the 10-year figure above assumes the return arrives smoothly, and it will not.

Now change one input. Suppose the deposit is needed in 3 years, not 10, and you have $45,000 today. The required return is (60,000 ÷ 45,000)^(1/3) − 1 = (1.333)^(0.333) − 1 = 10.1% a year, for three years running. That is above the long-run stock average with no room for a bad year, and a bad year within a three-year window is common. This goal is not compatible with a safe plan. The honest answers are: save more, buy a cheaper house, or wait. Loading up on risk is how people arrive at the closing date with $38,000.

Why the horizon decides

Think about what a 35% fall does to each of the two plans above.

In the 10-year plan, a 35% fall in year 3 takes a balance of roughly $26,000 down to about $17,000. Ugly, but you have seven years and $21,000 of further contributions ahead of you, and those contributions buy at lower prices. The plan survives if you do.

In the 3-year plan, a 35% fall in year 2 takes $50,000 to $32,500 with one year left. No plausible return closes that gap. The plan is dead, and the only thing that would have saved it is not having been exposed to the fall in the first place.

Same event, same percentage, opposite outcomes. The difference is entirely the horizon. This is why the standard advice ties equity exposure to time: not because stocks are guaranteed to recover within any particular window, but because the longer the window, the more likely recovery is to arrive before the money is needed, and the more contributions you will make at depressed prices along the way.

Table

A simple way to hold this in your head is to split money by when it is needed and give each bucket a different job.

Horizon Job of the money Tolerable temporary fall Typical building blocks
0 to 2 years Be there, in full, on the date Near zero Treasury bills, money market funds, high-yield savings
2 to 5 years Beat inflation without a large loss 10% to 15% Short and intermediate bond funds, some broad equity
5 to 10 years Grow, with time to recover from one bad cycle 20% to 30% Balanced mix of broad equity and bond funds
10+ years Compound; volatility is the price of return 40% or more Mostly broad equity funds, small bond allocation

The percentages are ranges, not rules. The point of the table is the structure: the same person can sensibly hold near-cash for next year's tuition and a mostly-equity portfolio for retirement, because those are two different goals with two different horizons. Mixing them into one account with one allocation gets both wrong.

What goes in the plan, and what does not

A position belongs in a portfolio when you can say, in one sentence, what job it does toward the goal. "Broad US equity exposure for long-run growth." "Bonds to cap the drawdown at a level I can hold through." "Cash for the deposit due in eighteen months." If the only sentence you can write is "I think it will go up," it is a trade, and trades live in a separate, bounded part of the account or not at all.

This does not mean single stocks are forbidden. It means they need a stated reason and a size limit, which is what lessons 5 through 7 cover.

Before the next lesson

Write your goal as three numbers: an amount, a date and a maximum tolerable temporary fall in both percent and dollars. Then compute the required return using the formula above. If it comes out above 8% or so, revisit the inputs before you go any further, because the rest of this course assumes a goal that is reachable without heroics.

Sources

  • U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov, "Asset Allocation": https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/getting-started/asset-allocation
  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern, "Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills: 1928–2023": https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/histretSP.html
  • Vanguard Research, "Vanguard's Principles for Investing Success": https://corporate.vanguard.com/content/dam/corp/research/pdf/Principles-for-investing-success.pdf
  • U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov, Compound Interest Calculator: https://www.investor.gov/financial-tools-calculators/calculators/compound-interest-calculator

quiz.q: What most clearly separates a portfolio from a pile of trades?
opts: The number of positions it holds
Whether it was built against a stated goal, horizon and risk budget
Whether it is up or down this year
quiz.explain: A pile accumulates by accident. A portfolio is designed backwards from a goal, a date and a tolerable loss, and every position has to justify its place against those three things.

quiz.q: You need $60,000 in 10 years, start with $15,000 and can add $3,000 a year. Roughly what annual return does the goal require?
quiz.explain: At 4% the plan reaches about $58,200 and at 5% about $62,200, so the required return sits near 4.5%. That is well below the long-run return of an all-stock portfolio, which means the goal does not force you to take full equity risk.

quiz.q: Why does time horizon matter more than expected return when choosing how much risk to take?
opts: A short horizon leaves no time to recover from a large drawdown before the money is needed
Brokers charge less for long-term accounts
Horizon determines which tickers are available
quiz.explain: The market does not know when you need the money. If a 35% fall lands two years before a fixed spending date, there may not be time to recover, so the horizon caps how much drawdown you can accept.

quiz.q: Which of these is a well-specified portfolio goal?
opts: Make as much money as possible
Accumulate $60,000 by September 2036 for a house deposit, accepting no more than a 25% temporary fall
quiz.explain: A usable goal has an amount, a date and a stated tolerance for loss. Without all three you cannot compute a required return or decide whether a given allocation is acceptable.

quiz.q: Using Damodaran's 1928 to 2023 data, the long-run geometric return of the S&P 500 was roughly what, in nominal terms?
quiz.explain: The compounded annual return was about 9.8% nominal over that period, versus about 4.9% for 10-year Treasuries and 3.3% for Treasury bills. Those are averages across many very different decades, not a promise for the next ten years.

content.heading: Risk, Return, and the Risks Volatility Misses
content.body:
Two returns, one that matters

When someone says a fund "averaged 8%," ask which average. There are two, and the gap between them is where a lot of disappointment lives.

The arithmetic mean adds up the yearly returns and divides by the number of years. It is what you get from a calculator and what marketing tends to quote.

The geometric mean is the constant annual rate that would have turned the starting balance into the ending balance. It is what your account actually experienced. It is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean, and the gap grows with volatility.

For a set of yearly returns r₁, r₂ … rₙ:

  • Arithmetic: (r₁ + r₂ + … + rₙ) ÷ n
  • Geometric: [(1 + r₁)(1 + r₂)…(1 + rₙ)]^(1/n) − 1

A useful approximation links them: geometric ≈ arithmetic − σ² ÷ 2, where σ is the standard deviation of the yearly returns. This term, half the variance, is called volatility drag. It is not a rounding error; for volatile assets it is several percentage points a year.

Worked example

Two portfolios, each starting at $10,000.

Portfolio A returns 8% every single year.

Portfolio B alternates: +38% in odd years, −22% in even years. Its arithmetic average is (38 − 22) ÷ 2 = 8%, the same as A.

Geometric return of B. Every two years B is multiplied by 1.38 × 0.78 = 1.0764. The annual rate is √1.0764 = 1.0375, so B compounds at 3.75% a year, not 8%.

Check with the approximation. B's returns are 38% and −22% around a mean of 8%, so each is 30 points from the mean. Standard deviation is 30%, variance is 0.09, and half the variance is 0.045. Arithmetic 8% minus 4.5% gives 3.5%, close to the exact 3.75%.

Ten-year balances.

  • A: 10,000 × 1.08^10 = 10,000 × 2.1589 = $21,589
  • B: 10,000 × 1.0764^5 = 10,000 × 1.4453 = $14,453

Same "average return," a $7,100 gap. Nothing about B was hidden; the arithmetic average simply describes a number that never compounds.

One more step: what if B's bad year were −30% instead of −22%? The arithmetic average is still respectable at (38 − 30) ÷ 2 = 4%. But 1.38 × 0.70 = 0.966 per two years, so B now loses 1.7% a year and ends ten years at $8,415. A small increase in the size of the bad years turns a positive average into a shrinking account. This is the arithmetic of why capping losses matters more than chasing gains, and it comes back in lesson 9.

What standard deviation measures, and what it does not

Standard deviation, usually called volatility, measures how widely returns scatter around their average. For a portfolio with an 8% mean and 15% standard deviation, roughly two years in three land between −7% and +23%, and about one year in twenty lands outside −22% to +38%, if returns were normally distributed. They are not quite, and the tails are fatter than the bell curve implies, but the shape is a serviceable first picture.

To convert daily volatility to annual, multiply by the square root of the number of trading days, about 252. A stock with 2% daily standard deviation has 2% × √252 ≈ 32% annual volatility. Monthly figures multiply by √12.

Volatility is a genuinely useful number. It is the input to the diversification arithmetic in the next lesson, it drives the drag term above, and it scales roughly with how bad a bad year can be. But it has blind spots, and a beginner who tracks only volatility will be surprised by every one of them.

It treats up and down alike. A stock that jumps 20% on good news adds as much to volatility as one that falls 20%. You care about the second.

It says nothing about permanence. A broad index fund that falls 30% and a single company that falls 30% have the same volatility that month. The index has always recovered eventually; the company may be on its way to zero. Hendrik Bessembinder's 2018 study of every US-listed stock from 1926 to 2016 found that the majority of individual stocks earned less than one-month Treasury bills over their lifetimes, and that all of the net wealth creation above bills came from about 4% of them. Volatility does not distinguish the 4% from the rest.

It ignores the order of returns. Two sequences with identical volatility and identical geometric return can produce very different outcomes for someone who is adding or withdrawing money along the way. This is sequence risk, and it is the reason the horizon in lesson 1 matters.

It ignores whether you can sell. A private investment, a thinly traded small-cap or a crypto token on an exchange that halts withdrawals can show low volatility right up until the moment you need the cash and there is no bid.

It ignores leverage. A position bought on margin has the same volatility as one bought with cash, but a fall that a cash holder can wait out can force a margin holder to sell at the bottom.

Table

Risk What it is How you see it How you limit it
Volatility Width of the range of outcomes Standard deviation of returns Diversification, bond allocation
Drawdown Peak-to-trough fall, however long it takes Max drawdown, time to recover Allocation sized to the risk budget
Permanent loss A holding that never comes back Single-name bankruptcies, delistings Position limits, broad funds in the core
Concentration Too much riding on one name, sector or theme Largest position as % of total Hard cap per position, look-through check
Sequence Bad years landing when money is added or withdrawn Outcome depends on order of returns Shorter-horizon money in lower-risk buckets
Liquidity Unable to sell at a fair price when needed Wide spreads, halted trading Prefer listed, high-volume holdings for money you may need
Inflation Purchasing power falls while nominal value holds Real return below zero Do not hold long-horizon money entirely in cash
Leverage Losses can exceed what you can wait out Margin calls, forced sales No margin in a first portfolio

Each row is a separate thing to check. A portfolio can have low volatility and high concentration risk (one stable-looking stock), or high volatility and low permanent-loss risk (a broad small-cap index). You want a view of all of them, not one number.

Return has to be judged against risk taken

Two portfolios that both returned 10% last year did not necessarily do equally well. If one had 8% volatility and the other 25%, the first delivered the same result with a much narrower range of things that could have gone wrong. The standard way to express this is the Sharpe ratio: excess return over the risk-free rate, divided by volatility. A 10% return with a 4% risk-free rate and 8% volatility gives (10 − 4) ÷ 8 = 0.75. The same return with 25% volatility gives 0.24. Lesson 11 comes back to this in detail; for now, the habit to build is never to look at a return without asking what risk bought it.

The same logic runs the other way. A portfolio that fell 12% in a year when the broad market fell 25% did its job if the job was to lose less. Judging it as a failure because the sign was negative is the mistake that pushes people into more risk right at the wrong moment.

What this means for construction

Three practical consequences follow from the arithmetic in this lesson.

First, expected return is not the only thing you are buying. Every unit of volatility costs you about half its square in compounded return, so a portfolio that gives up a little average return to cut volatility substantially can end up ahead in dollars. This is the mathematical case for diversification, and the next lesson puts numbers on it.

Second, the big losses dominate. The −22% versus −30% comparison above showed how a modest change in the depth of bad years flips the sign of the compounded result. Rules that cap losses, such as position sizing and rebalancing, are not conservatism for its own sake; they protect the compounding.

Third, track more than one risk. Before you buy anything, be able to say what its volatility is, how far it has fallen from a peak before, whether it can go to zero, how much of your total it would be, and whether you could sell it on a bad day. If you cannot answer those five questions, you do not yet know what you are buying.

Sources

  • Hendrik Bessembinder, "Do Stocks Outperform Treasury Bills?", Journal of Financial Economics 129(3), 2018: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2018.06.004
  • William F. Sharpe, "The Sharpe Ratio", Journal of Portfolio Management 21(1), 1994: https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.1994.409501
  • U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov, "What Is Risk?": https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/what-risk
  • FINRA, "Asset Allocation and Diversification": https://www.finra.org/investors/investing/investing-basics/asset-allocation-diversification

quiz.q: Portfolio A returns exactly 8% every year. Portfolio B alternates +38% and −22%, which also averages 8%. After ten years, which is worth more?
opts: They are equal because the average is the same
B, because it has bigger up years
A, because the geometric return of B is only about 3.75% a year
It depends on which year B starts with
quiz.explain: What compounds is the geometric return, not the arithmetic average. B's two-year growth factor is 1.38 × 0.78 = 1.0764, which is about 3.75% a year. Over ten years A grows to 2.16x and B to only 1.45x.

quiz.q: Roughly how much does volatility reduce the compounded return relative to the arithmetic average?
quiz.explain: Geometric return is approximately arithmetic return minus half the variance. With a 30% standard deviation the drag is about 0.09 ÷ 2 = 4.5 percentage points a year.

quiz.q: Which of these risks is NOT captured by the standard deviation of returns?
opts: The chance that a single company goes to zero and never recovers
The width of the range of annual outcomes
How much the portfolio bounced last month
quiz.explain: Standard deviation measures dispersion around an average and treats up and down moves alike. Permanent loss, liquidity, sequence risk and concentration are different things and need to be tracked separately.

quiz.q: Bessembinder (2018) found that over 1926 to 2016, net wealth creation in the US stock market above Treasury bills came from roughly what share of listed stocks?
quiz.explain: About 4% of stocks accounted for all of the net gain above T-bills; the majority of individual stocks earned less than T-bills over their lifetimes. Diversification is what captures the winners you cannot pick in advance.

quiz.q: If a stock's daily return standard deviation is 2%, its approximate annualised volatility is
quiz.explain: Annualise by multiplying by the square root of the number of trading days: 2% × √252 ≈ 2% × 15.9 ≈ 32%.

content.heading: Diversification and Correlation
content.body:
Why diversification is arithmetic, not opinion

Harry Markowitz's 1952 paper made one observation that still runs every serious portfolio: the risk of a portfolio is not the average risk of its holdings. It depends on how the holdings move together. Two assets that each swing 20% can combine into something that swings 20%, 14%, or almost nothing, depending on one number: their correlation.

Correlation runs from −1 to +1. At +1 two assets move in lockstep and combining them changes nothing. At 0 their moves are unrelated and some cancel. At −1 they move exactly opposite and the right mix cancels everything. Real assets sit mostly between 0 and +0.9, and the interesting work of building a portfolio happens in that range.

This lesson gives you the formula, works it with real tickers, and then explains the two ways correlation will disappoint you if you trust a single historical number.

The formula

For two assets with weights w₁ and w₂, volatilities σ₁ and σ₂, and correlation ρ:

Portfolio variance = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² + 2 w₁ w₂ ρ σ₁ σ₂

Portfolio volatility is the square root of that.

For n assets held in equal weights, each with volatility σ and average pairwise correlation ρ, the formula collapses to:

Portfolio variance = (1 ÷ n) σ² + (1 − 1 ÷ n) ρ σ²

Look at what happens as n grows. The first term shrinks toward zero; that is the diversifiable part. The second term approaches ρσ². So no matter how many holdings you add, volatility never falls below σ√ρ. The count of holdings removes the first term. Only low correlation lowers the floor.

Worked example

Take five large technology stocks: AAPL, MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN and NVDA. Using daily returns over 2019 to 2023 and rounding, their annualised volatilities ran from roughly 30% (MSFT, AAPL) to 50% (NVDA), and their average pairwise correlation was about 0.6. To keep the arithmetic clean, use 35% volatility for each and ρ = 0.6. Your own figures will differ with the window; the shape of the result will not.

Equal-weight portfolio of the five:

  • First term: (1 ÷ 5) × 0.35² = 0.2 × 0.1225 = 0.0245
  • Second term: (1 − 0.2) × 0.6 × 0.1225 = 0.8 × 0.0735 = 0.0588
  • Variance: 0.0245 + 0.0588 = 0.0833
  • Volatility: √0.0833 = 28.9%

Five stocks at 35% each produced a portfolio at 28.9%. You removed about six points of volatility, and the floor for this group is 0.35 × √0.6 = 27.1%. Adding a sixth, tenth or fiftieth tech stock would take you from 28.9% toward 27.1% and no further. That is what "five tech stocks are not diversified" means in numbers: they share a driver, so they share most of their risk.

Same five volatilities, but stocks from five different sectors with ρ = 0.2:

  • First term: 0.0245 (unchanged)
  • Second term: 0.8 × 0.2 × 0.1225 = 0.0196
  • Variance: 0.0441
  • Volatility: √0.0441 = 21.0%

Same count, same individual volatilities, eight points less portfolio volatility, and the floor is now 0.35 × √0.2 = 15.7%. The difference between 28.9% and 21.0% came entirely from correlation.

Add a bond fund. Now take a two-asset mix: 80% in the five-sector stock basket (21.0% volatility) and 20% in BND, the Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF, with roughly 5% volatility and correlation to stocks of about 0.1 over 2010 to 2021.

  • w₁²σ₁² = 0.64 × 0.0441 = 0.02822
  • w₂²σ₂² = 0.04 × 0.0025 = 0.00010
  • Cross term: 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 × 0.1 × 0.21 × 0.05 = 0.000336
  • Variance: 0.02866
  • Volatility: √0.02866 = 16.9%

A 20% bond allocation took the portfolio from 21.0% to 16.9%. Lesson 2 showed that volatility drag is half the variance, so this also lifts the compounded return relative to the arithmetic return by about (0.0441 − 0.0287) ÷ 2 = 0.77 points a year, partially offsetting the lower expected return of bonds.

Table

Approximate correlations of daily returns, 2019 to 2023, rounded to one decimal. Compute your own before relying on any of them.

AAPL MSFT GOOGL AMZN NVDA SPY BND
AAPL 1.0 0.7 0.6 0.6 0.6 0.8 0.1
MSFT 0.7 1.0 0.7 0.6 0.6 0.8 0.1
GOOGL 0.6 0.7 1.0 0.6 0.5 0.7 0.1
AMZN 0.6 0.6 0.6 1.0 0.5 0.7 0.1
NVDA 0.6 0.6 0.5 0.5 1.0 0.7 0.0
SPY 0.8 0.8 0.7 0.7 0.7 1.0 0.1
BND 0.1 0.1 0.1 0.1 0.0 0.1 1.0

Two things to read off the table. First, each of the five stocks correlates more strongly with SPY than with the others, because the index is what they have in common; a holder of all five has largely bought the index with extra single-name noise. Second, BND sits near zero against everything, which is the property that made the bond calculation above work.

How many stocks is enough

Evans and Archer, in 1968, found that most of the diversifiable variance was gone by about 10 randomly chosen stocks. Meir Statman revisited the question in 1987 with a cost-benefit framing and put the figure at 30 to 40. Campbell, Lettau, Malkiel and Xu showed in 2001 that individual-stock volatility had roughly doubled between the 1960s and the 1990s while market volatility had not, so the number of stocks required to reach a given level of diversification had risen to around 50.

The practical reading for a first portfolio: a handful of individual stocks does not diversify you, and even ten do not fully. That is not an argument against holding single names. It is the argument for putting a broad fund at the core, which gives you the 500 or 3,500 names at once, and treating individual stocks as bounded additions on top. Lesson 6 is built on that split.

Two ways correlation will let you down

Correlations rise when markets fall. François Longin and Bruno Solnik, using 38 years of monthly data across international equity markets, showed that correlation increases in large negative moves and not in large positive ones. Andrew Ang and Joseph Chen found the same asymmetry within US stocks. In October 2008, almost every equity market, most commodities and most credit fell together; the 0.6 in the table above was closer to 0.9 that month. Diversification across stocks reduces ordinary, day-to-day volatility. It offers much less protection against the event you most want protection from. Only assets with a genuinely different driver, such as Treasury bonds and cash, kept their value that year.

Correlations change regime. The SPY–TLT correlation, roughly −0.3 over 2010 to 2020, turned positive in 2022, when the S&P 500 lost 18.1% and TLT lost over 30% because both were repriced by the same rise in interest rates. Anyone who had sized their bond allocation on the assumption that bonds always rise when stocks fall was surprised twice. A correlation estimate is a description of a window of history, and the regime that produced it can end.

The defence against both is the same: do not build a portfolio whose survival depends on a correlation staying where it was. Size positions so that if everything falls together, the total fall is still inside your risk budget from lesson 1. Treat the diversification benefit as a bonus in normal times, not as the load-bearing wall.

What to do with this

Before you add any holding, ask what it correlates with. If the answer is "the things I already own," you are adding size, not diversification. If you cannot answer, compute it: three years of monthly returns and a spreadsheet correlation function take five minutes.

Then remember that the number you computed is a snapshot. Assume it will be higher in a crash, and check that the portfolio still fits your budget when it is.

Sources

  • Harry Markowitz, "Portfolio Selection", Journal of Finance 7(1), 1952: https://www.jstor.org/stable/2975974
  • Meir Statman, "How Many Stocks Make a Diversified Portfolio?", Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 22(3), 1987: https://www.jstor.org/stable/2330969
  • John Y. Campbell, Martin Lettau, Burton G. Malkiel and Yexiao Xu, "Have Individual Stocks Become More Volatile?", Journal of Finance 56(1), 2001: https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00318
  • François Longin and Bruno Solnik, "Extreme Correlation of International Equity Markets", Journal of Finance 56(2), 2001: https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00340

quiz.q: Five stocks each have 35% volatility. If their average pairwise correlation is 0.6, the equal-weight portfolio's volatility is closest to
quiz.explain: Portfolio variance = (1/5)(0.35²) + (4/5)(0.6)(0.35²) = 0.0245 + 0.0588 = 0.0833, so volatility is √0.0833 ≈ 28.9%. Five tech stocks remove only about six points of volatility.

quiz.q: As the number of equally weighted holdings grows very large, portfolio volatility approaches
opts: The volatility of the largest holding
quiz.explain: The 1/n term vanishes and what remains is ρ × σ², so the floor is σ × √ρ. With ρ = 0.6 and σ = 35% the floor is about 27%; with ρ = 0.2 it is about 15.7%. Correlation, not count, sets the floor.

quiz.q: Which statement about correlation in market crises is supported by the research cited in this lesson?
opts: Correlations between stocks fall sharply in crashes, helping diversification
Correlations between equity markets rise in large down moves, so diversification across stocks helps least when needed most
quiz.explain: Longin and Solnik (2001) and Ang and Chen (2002) both document that correlations rise in large negative moves. Diversification across stocks reduces ordinary volatility but does not protect against a broad crash; only assets with genuinely different drivers do that.

quiz.q: Between 2010 and 2020 the correlation of SPY and TLT daily returns was roughly negative. In 2022 it turned positive. What does this tell you?
opts: Correlation is an estimate from a window of data and can change when the driver of returns changes, so a plan must not depend on a single historical value
The 60/40 portfolio can never lose money
quiz.explain: In 2022 both stocks and long bonds fell because rising rates hit both at once. A diversifier's value depends on the regime; you should assume correlations can move against you and size accordingly.

quiz.q: Statman (1987) and Campbell, Lettau, Malkiel and Xu (2001) suggest roughly how many stocks are needed to remove most diversifiable risk?
quiz.explain: Statman put the figure at 30 to 40 for a well-diversified portfolio; Campbell and co-authors found that rising idiosyncratic volatility had pushed the number to around 50 by the late 1990s. A ten-stock portfolio still carries meaningful single-name risk unless the core is a broad fund.

content.heading: Asset Classes and What Each Does
content.body:
An asset class is a return driver

An asset class is a group of holdings whose returns come from the same underlying source. Stocks are paid by corporate profits. Bonds are paid by contractual interest and the return of principal. Cash is paid by short-term interest rates. Real estate is paid by rents. Commodities are paid by nobody; their return is entirely price change.

This matters because the previous lesson showed that correlation sets the floor on portfolio risk, and correlation comes from shared drivers. Two things paid by the same source will move together. So the way to get genuinely low correlation is to hold assets paid by different sources, which is what mixing asset classes does. Owning fifty stocks diversifies you across companies. Owning stocks and bonds diversifies you across drivers.

Below is what each class does, what it costs you in the bad years, and where the two things beginners most often ask about, options and crypto, fit.

Stocks

Stocks are ownership claims on businesses. Over long periods they have returned more than any other liquid asset class: about 9.8% a year compounded for the S&P 500 from 1928 to 2023 in Aswath Damodaran's data, before inflation and costs. That return is compensation for two things: profits are uncertain, and stockholders are paid last.

The cost of the return is the drawdown. The S&P 500 fell about 37% in calendar 2008, 43% in 1931, and 18% in 2022. Peak to trough, it has lost half its value three times since 2000. Any allocation to stocks has to be made knowing that a 50% fall is a normal event over a multi-decade horizon, not a black swan.

Within stocks, the main sub-divisions are by geography (US, developed international, emerging), by size (large, mid, small) and by style (value, growth). Each carries a somewhat different mix of drivers, and the correlations between them sit around 0.7 to 0.9 rather than 1.0, so holding several helps a little. The cheapest way to hold all of them at once is a total-market fund: VTI covers roughly 3,500 US stocks at a 0.03% expense ratio, and VXUS covers about 8,000 non-US stocks at 0.05%, as of their 2025 prospectuses.

Job in the portfolio: long-run growth. What it costs you: the deepest drawdowns of any liquid class.

Bonds

A bond is a loan. You hand over principal, the borrower pays interest on a schedule and returns the principal at maturity. Because the payments are contractual, a bond's return is far more predictable than a stock's, provided the borrower pays. US Treasuries carry essentially no default risk; corporate bonds carry some and pay extra yield for it.

The risk bonds do carry is interest-rate risk. When market rates rise, existing bonds with lower coupons become less valuable, and the longer the bond's remaining life, the larger the move. This is measured by duration: a fund with a duration of 6 years loses roughly 6% of its price for every one-point rise in yields. 2022 was the demonstration. The Federal Reserve raised rates faster than at any time since the early 1980s, the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index fell 13.0%, and long-Treasury funds like TLT fell over 30%. Bonds are lower-risk than stocks; they are not risk-free, and they are least safe precisely when their duration is long.

The reason to hold them anyway is the correlation. Over most of 2000 to 2021, Treasury bonds rose when stocks fell, because the same recessions that hurt profits pushed rates down. In 2008 the Aggregate index returned +5.2% while the S&P 500 returned −37%. Even in 2022, when both fell, an intermediate bond fund fell less than stocks. BND, the Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF, holds about 11,000 investment-grade bonds with a duration near 6 years at 0.03%.

Job in the portfolio: cap the drawdown, provide something to sell to buy stocks after a crash. What it costs you: lower long-run return, and losses when rates rise fast.

Cash

Cash means Treasury bills, money-market funds and high-yield savings, not a checking account. It has never had a negative nominal calendar year. Its return is whatever short rates are: near zero in 2021, over 5% in 2023.

The risk is inflation. In 2022 T-bills returned about 2% while consumer prices rose about 6.5%, so cash lost roughly 4.5% of its purchasing power. Over a decade of 3% inflation, a cash holding earning 1% loses about 18% of its real value without a single red day.

Job in the portfolio: money needed within about two years, and dry powder for rebalancing. What it costs you: guaranteed erosion by inflation if held too long. Funds like SGOV (0.09%) or BIL hold T-bills directly.

Real estate, commodities and gold

Listed real estate (REITs) is paid by rents and carries stock-like volatility with a correlation to broad stocks around 0.6 to 0.7. It is a modest diversifier, and a total-market fund already includes it at roughly its market weight. Commodities have no cash flow; their return is price change plus the cost of rolling futures contracts, which has historically been a drag. Gold is the special case: no cash flow, but a long record of holding value in currency crises and low correlation with stocks. It also fell 28% in calendar 2013 and has gone two decades without a new high before. If you hold it, hold it small, and know that you are paying 0.25% to 0.40% a year (IAU, GLD) for an asset that pays nothing.

Options: a tool, not an asset class

An option is a contract that gives its buyer the right, and its seller the obligation, to trade an underlying asset at a fixed price before an expiry date. It is not an asset class because it does not have its own return driver; it repackages the underlying's risk and adds a clock.

Two uses are legitimate in a portfolio context. Buying a put on an index fund is insurance against a fall; it costs a premium every time you renew it, and over long periods that premium is a persistent drag, so it is a choice about paying to limit drawdown, not a free lunch. Selling a covered call on a holding you own produces premium income in exchange for giving up gains above the strike; it caps your upside on that position and does nothing to protect the downside beyond the premium received.

Everything else, meaning buying calls or puts for directional bets, is trading, not portfolio construction, and belongs in the bounded satellite sleeve from lesson 6 or nowhere. The SEC's investor bulletin on options is the right place to learn the mechanics before you touch either use.

Crypto: a high-volatility satellite at most

Crypto-assets have no cash flow and no agreed valuation model; their return is entirely what the next buyer pays. Bitcoin's annualised volatility has typically run 60% to 80%, three to four times that of the S&P 500, and its drawdowns have been of a different order: roughly −77% from the November 2021 peak near $69,000 to the November 2022 trough near $16,000, and about −83% in 2018. Correlation with stocks was near zero before 2020 and rose to around 0.4 to 0.6 in 2022, so it did not diversify a stock portfolio when that mattered.

The SEC's investor alerts on crypto-asset securities also flag risks that have nothing to do with price: exchange failures, custody loss and fraud. If you decide to hold any, the portfolio logic is the same as for any single high-volatility bet: a small fixed percentage, sized so that a 100% loss is survivable, and no rebalancing into it after a fall. Five percent of a portfolio going to zero is a bad year. Thirty percent going to zero is a changed life.

Worked example

A 60/40 portfolio of SPY and AGG, using figures from 2010 to 2021: SPY annualised volatility about 18%, AGG about 5%, correlation about −0.1.

  • w₁²σ₁² = 0.36 × 0.0324 = 0.011664
  • w₂²σ₂² = 0.16 × 0.0025 = 0.000400
  • Cross term: 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × (−0.1) × 0.18 × 0.05 = −0.000432
  • Variance: 0.011632
  • Volatility: √0.011632 = 10.8%

The 40% bond sleeve took an 18% asset and produced a 10.8% portfolio: 60% of the stock exposure delivered 60% of the volatility, and the small negative correlation shaved a little more.

Now the 2022 regime. Correlation rose to about +0.5:

  • Cross term: 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × 0.5 × 0.18 × 0.05 = +0.002160
  • Variance: 0.011664 + 0.000400 + 0.002160 = 0.014224
  • Volatility: √0.014224 = 11.9%

And the actual 2022 return: 0.6 × (−18.1%) + 0.4 × (−13.0%) = −10.86% − 5.20% = −16.1%. Compare with 2008: 0.6 × (−37.0%) + 0.4 × (+5.2%) = −22.2% + 2.1% = −20.1%. The bond sleeve cut the 2008 loss by 17 points and the 2022 loss by only 2 points. Same allocation, different regime; the lesson is to expect the smaller benefit when sizing your risk budget, and treat the larger one as the good case.

Table

Asset class Return driver Typical annual volatility Worst calendar year, approx. Representative fund and expense ratio
US stocks Corporate profits 15% to 20% −43% (1931), −37% (2008) VTI, 0.03%
International stocks Profits, plus currency 16% to 22% −43% (2008, MSCI EAFE) VXUS, 0.05%
Investment-grade bonds Interest, principal 4% to 6% −13% (2022, US Aggregate) BND, 0.03%
Long Treasuries Interest, rate moves 12% to 15% −31% (2022, TLT) TLT, 0.15%
Cash / T-bills Short rates Under 1% No nominal loss; real loss ≈ −4.5% (2022) SGOV, 0.09%
Gold Price only 15% to 18% −28% (2013) IAU, 0.25%
Bitcoin Price only 60% to 80% −73% (2018), −64% (2022) IBIT, 0.25%

Volatility ranges are rounded from 2010 to 2023 data; worst years from index and fund histories. Expense ratios are from 2025 prospectuses and change; check before you buy.

The rule that comes out of this

Hold the classes that are paid by something, in proportions that keep the worst plausible year inside your risk budget. Use the classes that are paid by nothing, and the tools that expire, in small, bounded amounts with a written reason, or not at all. The next lesson turns "small, bounded amounts" into a formula.

Sources

  • U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov, "Options": https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/options
  • U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor Alert, "Exercise Caution with Crypto Asset Securities": https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-alerts/exercise-caution-crypto-asset
  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern, "Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills: 1928–2023": https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/histretSP.html

quiz.explain: 0.6 × (−18.1%) + 0.4 × (−13.0%) = −10.9% − 5.2% = −16.1%. Bonds cushioned less than usual because rising rates hit both asset classes in the same year.

quiz.q: What is the primary job of a bond allocation in a first portfolio?
opts: To cap the drawdown at a level the investor can hold through, using an asset with a different return driver
quiz.explain: Bonds carry contractual cash flows and usually low correlation with stocks. They reduce portfolio volatility and drawdown, though 2022 showed they are not immune to loss when rates rise sharply.

quiz.q: Options are best described as
opts: An asset class like stocks or bonds
Contracts on other assets that shift risk between buyer and seller and expire, so they are tools rather than long-term holdings
quiz.explain: An option is a right or obligation tied to an underlying asset with an expiry date. It can hedge or generate premium, but every option has a cost or an obligation on the other side and it decays to zero at expiry.

quiz.q: Bitcoin fell from about $69,000 in November 2021 to about $16,000 in November 2022. Roughly what percentage fall is that, and what gain is needed to recover it?
quiz.explain: (16,000 − 69,000) ÷ 69,000 = −76.8%. Recovering from a 76.8% fall requires a gain of 0.768 ÷ 0.232 = 331%. This is why any crypto allocation in a first portfolio belongs in a small, bounded satellite if it belongs at all.

quiz.q: Which asset class has had no nominal calendar-year loss but loses purchasing power to inflation?
opts: Treasury bills and money market funds
quiz.explain: T-bills have positive nominal returns every year, but in years when inflation exceeds their yield the real return is negative. Cash is the right holding for short-horizon money and the wrong one for long-horizon money.

content.heading: Position Sizing
content.body:
The question sizing answers

You have decided a holding belongs in the portfolio. The next question is how much, and it is the question beginners skip most often. They decide whether to buy, then buy an amount that feels right: $1,000 because it is round, or 100 shares because that is a lot, or "about the same as the others." None of those is a sizing rule, and the absence of a rule is how one position ends up at 35% of the account.

Sizing is the mechanism that connects the risk budget from lesson 1 to the individual positions. There are two families of rule. Both work. The mistake is to use neither.

Fixed-fractional sizing

The simplest rule: each position is a fixed percentage of current account value. Ten positions at 10% each, or a core fund at 60% and eight satellites at 5% each. When you add money or the account grows, the percentages stay the same and the dollars scale.

Fixed-fractional sizing is self-correcting in a drawdown. If the account falls 20%, every new position is sized 20% smaller in dollars, which is what you want when things are going badly. It also has a built-in cap: no position can exceed its fraction at purchase, and rebalancing (lesson 8) pulls it back if it grows past.

What fixed-fractional does not do is adjust for how risky each holding is. A 10% position in a bond fund and a 10% position in a small biotech are the same dollars and very different risks. For the core of a portfolio, where the holdings are broad funds, this does not matter much. For individual stocks it does, which is what the second family handles.

Risk-per-trade sizing

The risk-per-trade rule starts from the loss you will accept on this one position if it goes wrong, and works backwards to the number of shares.

Shares = (Account value × Risk per position) ÷ (Entry price − Stop price)

The "risk per position" is typically 1% to 2% of the account. The stop is the price at which you have decided, in advance, that the reason you bought no longer holds. The distance from entry to stop is your risk per share. Divide the dollar risk by the risk per share and you have the position size.

This is the "1% rule" or "2% rule." What it means is not "put 1% of the account in each stock." It means "size each position so that if it hits its stop, the account loses 1%." A wide stop produces a small position; a tight stop produces a large one.

Worked example

Account: $25,000. Risk per position: 1%, so $250. You want to buy a stock at $50 with a stop at $45.

Step 1: dollar risk. 25,000 × 0.01 = $250.

Step 2: risk per share. 50 − 45 = $5.

Step 3: shares. 250 ÷ 5 = 50 shares.

Step 4: position value. 50 × $50 = $2,500, which is 10% of the account.

If the stop is hit you lose 50 × $5 = $250, exactly 1%. If the stock instead rises to $60, you gain $500, 2% of the account, for a 2:1 payoff on the risk taken.

Now tighten the stop to $47.50. Risk per share is $2.50. Shares = 250 ÷ 2.50 = 100. Position value = $5,000, 20% of the account.

The risk-per-trade formula is satisfied: a stop at $47.50 loses $250. But the position is now a fifth of the account, and the formula's assumption is that you will get out at $47.50. Stocks gap. A company that reports bad earnings after the close can open 25% lower, and your stop executes at $37.50, a loss of $1,250 or 5% of the account. A fraud, a delisting or a halted stock can take the whole position.

So the second rule applies alongside the first: no position larger than a stated maximum weight, typically 5% to 15% for individual stocks in a first portfolio. With a 15% cap, the maximum here is $3,750 or 75 shares, regardless of what the stop formula says. You take the smaller of the two numbers, always.

What the two rules are protecting. The risk-per-trade rule protects against the ordinary case: the thesis was wrong and the stop takes you out with a small, planned loss. The weight cap protects against the extraordinary case: the exit you planned does not happen. Bessembinder's finding from lesson 2, that most individual stocks lose to T-bills over their lives, is the reason both are needed.

Why 1% to 2% and not more

The case for small per-position risk is a losing streak, and losing streaks are normal. A strategy with a 55% win rate will produce five consecutive losses about 1.8% of the time per sequence of five, which over a hundred positions means you should expect to see it. Ten in a row is rarer but not rare enough to ignore.

The table below shows what a run of ten losses does at different risk levels, and what gain is needed to get back to even afterwards.

Table

Risk per position Equity after 10 straight losses Gain needed to recover Equity after 20 straight losses
0.5% 0.995^10 = 95.1% 5.1% 90.5%
1% 0.99^10 = 90.4% 10.6% 81.8%
2% 0.98^10 = 81.7% 22.4% 66.8%
5% 0.95^10 = 59.9% 67.0% 35.8%
10% 0.90^10 = 34.9% 186.7% 12.2%

At 1%, ten losses in a row is a bad quarter you recover from. At 5% it is a catastrophe that requires a 67% gain just to get back to zero, and at 10% the account is functionally gone. The gap between 1% and 2% is real but survivable; the gap between 2% and 5% is the difference between a plan and a gamble.

The Kelly criterion, briefly

There is a formula for the position size that maximises long-run growth, derived by John Kelly in 1956 and applied to markets by Edward Thorp. For a bet that wins with probability p and pays b dollars per dollar risked when it wins:

Kelly fraction = p − (1 − p) ÷ b

With p = 0.55 and b = 1 (you win as much as you lose), the fraction is 0.55 − 0.45 ÷ 1 = 0.10, so 10% of the account risked per position.

That is far more than 1%. Two reasons practitioners do not use it. First, the formula assumes you know p and b, and you do not; you have estimated them from a small sample, and if the true win rate is 50% rather than 55%, the Kelly fraction is zero and betting 10% is destroying capital at the fastest possible rate. Second, even at the correct fraction, full Kelly produces drawdowns most people cannot hold: a 50% drawdown has meaningful probability. Half Kelly gives up about a quarter of the growth rate for roughly half the variance, and quarter Kelly is closer to what most disciplined traders actually run. The 1% to 2% rule is, in effect, a fractional Kelly for someone honest about not knowing their edge.

Putting the rules together

For the core: fixed-fractional. Decide the percentages, buy those percentages, rebalance back to them.

For each satellite position:

  1. Write the stop, meaning the price at which the reason for owning it is invalid.
  2. Compute shares from the 1% (or 2%) rule.
  3. Compute the maximum shares from the weight cap.
  4. Buy the smaller.
  5. Record the entry, the stop, the share count and the dollar risk in one line.

Step 5 is not clerical. A position whose stop is not written down does not have a stop; it has a hope. Lesson 10 covers why the written version is the only one that survives contact with a red screen, and lesson 12 makes the rules part of your plan.

Sources

  • J. L. Kelly Jr., "A New Interpretation of Information Rate", Bell System Technical Journal 35(4), 1956: https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1956.tb03809.x
  • Edward O. Thorp, "The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market", in Handbook of Asset and Liability Management, 2006: https://www.eecs.harvard.edu/cs286r/courses/fall12/papers/Thorpe_KellyCriterion2007.pdf
  • U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov, "Stop-Loss Order": https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/stop-loss-order
  • Hendrik Bessembinder, "Do Stocks Outperform Treasury Bills?", Journal of Financial Economics 129(3), 2018: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2018.06.004

quiz.q: Account $25,000, risk per position 1%, entry $50, stop $45. How many shares does the risk-per-trade formula give?
quiz.explain: Dollar risk = 25,000 × 1% = $250. Risk per share = 50 − 45 = $5. Shares = 250 ÷ 5 = 50, a $2,500 position or 10% of the account.

quiz.q: Same account and 1% risk, but the stop is at $47.50 (5% below entry). The formula gives 100 shares, a $5,000 position. Why should a maximum-weight cap still apply?
opts: Because 100 shares is an odd number
Because a tighter stop only limits the loss if the stop executes; a gap through the stop or a permanent-loss event exposes the full 20% weight
quiz.explain: Risk-per-trade sizing assumes the exit happens at the stop. Overnight gaps, halts and fraud do not honour stops, so a separate cap on position weight is the second line of defence.

quiz.q: After 10 consecutive losing positions, an account risking 1% per position retains about 90%. At 5% per position it retains about
quiz.explain: 0.95^10 = 0.599, so about 60% remains, and recovering needs a 67% gain. At 1% the recovery needed is only 11%. Small per-position risk keeps a losing streak survivable.

quiz.q: With a 55% win rate and 1:1 payoff, the full Kelly fraction is 10%. Why do most practitioners size at a fraction of Kelly?
opts: Because win rate and payoff are estimates; over-estimating them makes full Kelly ruinous, and half Kelly gives up little growth for far less variance
Because Kelly only works for coin flips
Because brokers cap position sizes at 5%
quiz.explain: Kelly maximises long-run growth only if the inputs are exactly right. Betting more than Kelly reduces growth and raises ruin risk sharply, so uncertainty about the inputs argues for staying well below it.

quiz.q: Fixed-fractional sizing means
opts: Buying a fixed number of shares each time
Each position is a fixed percentage of current account value, so size scales down after losses and up after gains
quiz.explain: Sizing to a fixed fraction of current equity is self-correcting: it automatically reduces exposure in a drawdown and increases it as the account grows.

content.heading: Core and Satellite Construction
content.body:
Two jobs, two sleeves

Everything so far has pointed the same way. Lesson 3 showed that a handful of stocks does not diversify you and that broad funds do. Lesson 4 showed that asset allocation, the split between stocks, bonds and cash, sets the drawdown. Lesson 5 showed that individual positions need a stop and a weight cap. Core-and-satellite is the structure that lets all three coexist in one account.

The core is the part of the portfolio that delivers the asset allocation. It holds broad, low-cost index funds in the proportions you decided in lesson 1, and it is left alone except to rebalance. It is where most of the money is, and it is boring by design.

The satellite sleeve is the part where you hold anything that is not the market: individual stocks, sector funds, a small gold or crypto position, a thematic bet. Each satellite has a written reason, a stop where relevant, and a weight cap. The sleeve as a whole has its own cap, typically 10% to 30% of the portfolio.

The split does two things at once. It guarantees that most of your money is diversified and cheap regardless of how the satellites turn out. And it gives you a bounded place to act on your own views, so that the urge to buy something does not end up reshaping the whole portfolio.

Why the core should be index funds

Three lines of evidence, none of them controversial.

Allocation explains most of the outcome. Brinson, Hood and Beebower, studying 91 large US pension funds over 1974 to 1983, found that the funds' asset allocation policy explained more than 90% of the variation in their returns over time. Security selection and market timing explained the remainder and, on average, reduced returns. Later work argued about the precise figure and about what "explain" means, but nobody has found that stock picking dominates. Get the allocation right first.

Most active managers underperform after costs. S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes the SPIVA scorecard twice a year, comparing active funds with their benchmarks. In the scorecards covering periods ending 2023, roughly 88% of actively managed US large-cap funds had underperformed the S&P 500 over 15 years, and the figure is similar or worse in most other categories. These are professionals with research budgets. Holding the index in the core means you at least match the thing most of them fail to beat.

Cost compounds against you. The SEC's investor bulletin on fees shows the arithmetic: a 1% annual fee on a portfolio earning 4% a year reduces the ending balance by about 28% over 20 years. Index funds covering the whole US market now cost 0.03% a year. There is no cheaper way to own the return driver.

What goes in the satellite sleeve

A satellite is any position you hold because you believe something the market price does not fully reflect. That belief has to be written down in a sentence you could later check: "Regional bank trades at 0.8x book value and I expect it to earn its way back to 1.2x within two years" is a thesis. "Great company" is not.

Sensible satellites for a first portfolio:

  • Individual stocks, each sized by the lesson 5 rules and capped at 5% or so.
  • A sector or factor fund, when you want tilt without single-name risk.
  • A small gold or crypto position, if at all, capped where a total loss is a bad month.
  • Cash held deliberately for a specific opportunity, with a date by which it goes back into the core if unused.

The sleeve cap matters as much as the per-position caps. Six satellites at 5% each is 30%, and if they are all technology stocks, lesson 3 says you have added one correlated 30% position, not six diversified ones. Check the sleeve's correlation with itself and with the core before you fill it.

Worked example

A $50,000 portfolio, 80% core and 20% satellite, for a ten-year goal with a risk budget of roughly a 30% drawdown.

Core: $40,000

  • VTI, US total stock market: 50%, $25,000, expense ratio 0.03%, annual cost 25,000 × 0.0003 = $7.50
  • VXUS, non-US total stock market: 15%, $7,500, expense ratio 0.05%, annual cost 7,500 × 0.0005 = $3.75
  • BND, US investment-grade bonds: 15%, $7,500, expense ratio 0.03%, annual cost 7,500 × 0.0003 = $2.25

Core annual fund cost: $7.50 + $3.75 + $2.25 = $13.50, a blended 0.034%.

Satellites: $10,000, four positions at 5% each, $2,500 apiece, each with a written thesis, a stop and the 5% cap.

Compare the cost with an alternative. The same $50,000 in an actively managed balanced fund at 0.70% costs $350 a year. Add a 1% advisory fee and the total is $850. Over 20 years at a 6% gross return, the difference between 0.03% and 1.7% in annual drag is:

  • 50,000 × 1.0597^20 = 50,000 × 3.191 = $159,550
  • 50,000 × 1.043^20 = 50,000 × 2.322 = $116,100

A $43,000 gap on a $50,000 start, from costs alone, before any difference in skill.

Now stress a satellite. One of the four positions loses 50%. Portfolio impact: 5% × 50% = 2.5%, or $1,250. Painful, survivable, and the other $48,750 is unaffected. Compare with a pile where that stock had drifted to 25% of the account: the same event costs 12.5%.

And stress the core. A 2008-type year: US stocks −37%, international stocks −43%, bonds +5%. Core return: 0.50 × (−37) + 0.15 × (−43) + 0.15 × (+5) = −18.5 − 6.45 + 0.75 = −24.2 points on the 80% core. If the satellites, being stocks, fall about 40%, that adds 0.20 × (−40) = −8.0 points. Portfolio: about −32%. That is right at the stated risk budget. If you could not hold through −32%, the fix is more bonds in the core, not fewer satellites, because the core is where the drawdown is set.

Table

Core Satellite
Share of portfolio 70% to 90% 10% to 30%
Holdings Broad index funds, 3 to 5 of them Individual stocks, sector funds, small alternatives
Reason to own Deliver the asset allocation A written thesis the market may not reflect
Cost 0.03% to 0.10% Varies; single stocks cost only the spread
Turnover Rebalance only, once or twice a year Bounded by stops and thesis reviews
Per-position cap Set by allocation 5% typical; never above 15%
What a 50% fall in one holding does Impossible for a broad fund in one holding −2.5% of portfolio at a 5% cap
Where the drawdown is set Here, by the stock/bond split Adds a few points at the sleeve cap

Deciding the split

The split between core and satellite is a statement about how much of your outcome you want to depend on your own judgement. At 90/10 the satellites are a hobby that cannot hurt you. At 70/30 they can move the result by several points a year in either direction. Above 70/30 you have a stock-picking portfolio with an index fund attached, and the evidence above says most people who run that arrangement would have done better without the picking.

A reasonable first setting is 80/20. Raise the satellite share only after a year in which your satellites, measured honestly by the method in lesson 11, beat the core they replaced. Lower it after a year in which they did not.

Before the next lesson

Write your target core allocation as three or four funds with percentages, and a satellite cap. Lesson 7 fills in the ten positions.

lessons_data.title: Building a 10-Position Portfolio Step by Step

content.heading: Building a 10-Position Portfolio Step by Step
content.body:
The build, in order

This lesson assembles everything into a concrete ten-position portfolio. The order matters. Beginners pick stocks first and discover the allocation afterwards; you will do it the other way round, because lesson 6 showed that allocation is where the result is decided.

The eight steps:

  1. Fix the amount, the horizon and the risk budget (lesson 1).
  2. Set the stock/bond/cash split that keeps the worst plausible year inside the budget (lesson 4).
  3. Fill the core with three or four broad funds (lesson 6).
  4. Choose satellites, each with a written thesis and a sector label.
  5. Size every position: fixed-fractional for the core, risk-per-trade plus weight cap for satellites (lesson 5).
  6. Check overlap and correlation, including look-through (lesson 3).
  7. Decide how to enter: at once or in stages.
  8. Record everything in one table.

Ten positions is the target because it is enough to hold a diversified core and five bounded satellites, and few enough that you can know every line. A first portfolio with forty positions is not more diversified; it is less understood.

Step 1 and 2: the budget and the split

Take a $20,000 portfolio, a ten-year horizon and a risk budget of a 30% temporary fall, which is $6,000. Lesson 4's arithmetic says a portfolio that is roughly 75% stocks and 25% bonds and cash lost about 25% to 30% in 2008-type conditions once satellites are included, so that is the split.

Step 3: the core

Sixty-five percent of the portfolio, four funds:

  • VTI, US total market, 30%.
  • VXUS, international total market, 15%.
  • BND, US investment-grade bonds, 15%.
  • SGOV, Treasury bills, 5%. This is the rebalancing reserve and the place new contributions wait until the next rebalance date.

The core alone is already a complete portfolio. If you stopped here you would hold about 11,000 stocks and 11,000 bonds for a blended cost near 0.04% a year. Everything that follows is optional.

Step 4: the satellites

Thirty-five percent in five positions at 7% each. The selection rule for a first portfolio is: five different sectors, each with a thesis you can write in one line and check in a year. For the example, using large, liquid names so that spreads and liquidity are not a concern:

  • JPM (financials): scale advantage in US banking; thesis is return on equity above peers persisting.
  • UNH (health care): managed-care scale; thesis is earnings growth in line with guidance.
  • XOM (energy): low-cost production and buybacks; thesis is free cash flow above dividends at $70 oil.
  • COST (consumer staples): membership model; thesis is renewal rates above 90% and steady comparable-store growth.
  • MSFT (technology): cloud share gains; thesis is Azure growth above 25% a year.

These are examples of the form a satellite list should take, not recommendations. Your five will be different, and they should be, because the thesis has to be one you hold.

Step 5: sizing

The core is fixed-fractional: the percentages above, in dollars.

Each satellite is 7% of $20,000, or $1,400. That is the weight cap. Now check it against the risk-per-trade rule. Suppose the account's per-position risk is 1.5%, or $300. A $1,400 position with a stop 20% below entry risks $280, inside the rule. A stop 30% below entry would risk $420, outside the rule; the fix is either a tighter stop, if the thesis supports one, or a smaller position of $1,000. Take the smaller of the two numbers, always.

Step 6: overlap and correlation

The five satellites are in five sectors, so their pairwise correlations are lower than five technology stocks would be, roughly 0.3 to 0.5 for large caps over 2019 to 2023 rather than 0.6. But every one of them is also inside VTI. The check that matters is look-through concentration: how much of the portfolio is in each company once the fund holdings are counted.

Worked example

$20,000 portfolio. Assumed prices are round numbers for arithmetic; use live quotes when you build your own.

Weight, dollars, assumed price, shares, and approximate annualised volatility for each line:

  1. VTI, core, broad US: 30%, $6,000, $300, 20 shares, 17%
  2. VXUS, core, broad ex-US: 15%, $3,000, $65, 46 shares, 17%
  3. BND, core, bonds: 15%, $3,000, $75, 40 shares, 5%
  4. SGOV, core, T-bills: 5%, $1,000, $100, 10 shares, 0.5%
  5. JPM, satellite, financials: 7%, $1,400, $250, 5.6 shares, 25%
  6. UNH, satellite, health care: 7%, $1,400, $350, 4 shares, 25%
  7. XOM, satellite, energy: 7%, $1,400, $110, 12.7 shares, 25%
  8. COST, satellite, consumer staples: 7%, $1,400, $900, 1.6 shares, 20%
  9. MSFT, satellite, technology: 7%, $1,400, $450, 3.1 shares, 25%
  10. Cash reserve, core: 0% at build, the destination for rounding remainders and dividends

Fractional shares are shown; if your broker does not support them, round down and leave the remainder in SGOV.

Look-through on Microsoft. Microsoft's weight in VTI was around 6% in 2024 to 2025 fund reports (check the current holdings page). Through VTI: 30% × 6% = 1.8%. Direct: 7%. Total exposure to one company: 8.8%. That is inside a 10% single-name look-through limit but it is worth knowing, because the direct MSFT position is not adding a new bet; it is increasing an existing one. The same check on JPM (about 1.3% of VTI) gives 0.4% + 7% = 7.4%.

Look-through on technology as a sector. Technology was roughly 30% of VTI in that period, so the core contributes 30% × 30% = 9%, plus the 7% in MSFT: about 16% of the portfolio in one sector. Reasonable, but if two more satellites were technology stocks the figure would be 30% and lesson 3's correlation floor would apply.

A simple risk number. The weighted average volatility ignores diversification, so it is an upper bound and easy to compute:

0.30 × 17 + 0.15 × 17 + 0.15 × 5 + 0.05 × 0.5 + 0.07 × (25 + 25 + 25 + 20 + 25) = 5.10 + 2.55 + 0.75 + 0.03 + 0.07 × 120 = 5.10 + 2.55 + 0.75 + 0.03 + 8.40 = 16.8%

True portfolio volatility, with correlations below 1, would be around 13% to 14%. Either figure is fine as a first risk number; what matters is that it is written down and compared with the same number next year.

The drawdown check. Apply a 2008-type year: US stocks −37%, international −43%, bonds +5%, T-bills +2%, satellites −40% on average.

0.30 × (−37) + 0.15 × (−43) + 0.15 × 5 + 0.05 × 2 + 0.35 × (−40) = −11.1 − 6.45 + 0.75 + 0.1 − 14.0 = −30.7%

That is $6,140 on $20,000, right at the risk budget. If that number would make you sell, move 10 points from VTI to BND now, while nothing is wrong. The check is cheap; the regret is not.

Step 7: entering

Vanguard's research on the question, most recently in 2023, found that investing a lump sum immediately beat spreading it over twelve months about 68% of the time across historical periods, because markets rise more often than they fall. The expected cost of waiting is modest, a fraction of a percent on average, and the benefit is behavioural: someone who would otherwise sit in cash for a year out of fear does better by averaging in over three months than by not investing.

The practical rule: enter the core at once, or over no more than three months if the idea of a bad first month would make you abandon the plan. Enter satellites one at a time as each thesis is written, not all on the same day.

Step 8: the record

Every position gets one line: ticker, sleeve, weight, dollars, shares, entry date, entry price, stop (satellites only), and the one-sentence reason. This record is what you rebalance against (lesson 8), measure against (lesson 11), and consult when a red day tempts you to change something (lesson 10). A portfolio without the record is a pile with better intentions.

Table

The build order as a checklist, with the lesson each step draws on and the number it produces.

Step Output Number to write down Lesson
Budget and horizon Amount, date, tolerable fall $6,000 / 30% 1
Allocation Stock/bond/cash split 75 / 20 / 5 4
Core 3 to 4 broad funds with weights 65% in four funds 6
Satellites 5 positions, 5 sectors, 5 theses 35% in five names 6
Sizing Dollars and shares per position 7% cap, ≤1.5% risk each 5
Overlap Look-through by name and sector MSFT 8.8%, tech 16% 3
Risk number Weighted volatility, drawdown check 16.8%, −30.7% 2, 4
Entry and record Dates, prices, stops One line per position 7

Sources

  • U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov, "Asset Allocation": https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/getting-started/asset-allocation

  • Meir Statman, "How Many Stocks Make a Diversified Portfolio?", Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 22(3), 1987: https://www.jstor.org/stable/2330969

content.heading: Rebalancing
content.body:
Why weights drift

You set an allocation in lesson 7. Within a year it will be wrong, not because you did anything but because the holdings moved at different rates. Stocks rise 25%, bonds fall 5%, and the 60/40 portfolio you built is now 66/34. Keep going and the drift compounds: Vanguard's research shows that a 60/40 US portfolio left untouched from 1926 would have drifted to over 80% stocks, with the volatility and drawdown of a much more aggressive allocation than the one its owner chose.

Rebalancing is the act of selling what has grown and buying what has shrunk to restore the target weights. It is the maintenance step that keeps the risk budget from lesson 1 in force.

What rebalancing is for, and what it is not for

It is for risk control. The allocation was set so that the worst plausible year stayed inside your budget. Drift toward the higher-risk asset silently raises that worst year. Rebalancing puts it back.

It is not primarily for return. Because the asset that drifts upward is usually the one with the higher expected return, rebalancing typically gives up a little return relative to letting winners run. Vanguard's rebalancing studies found that over long periods a rebalanced 60/40 had somewhat lower return and substantially lower volatility than an unrebalanced one. There are periods where rebalancing adds return, when assets mean-revert, but you should not count on a "rebalancing bonus." Count on the risk control.

It is also a forced discipline. Rebalancing sells after a rise and buys after a fall, which is the opposite of what your instincts will tell you to do. In March 2009 or March 2020 the rebalancing rule said to sell bonds and buy stocks. The people who followed a written rule did; the people who relied on judgement mostly did not.

Calendar versus threshold

Calendar rebalancing checks and trades on a fixed schedule: every quarter, every six months, every year. It is simple and easy to automate. The cost is that it can trade when the drift is trivial, incurring tax and transaction cost for nothing, and it can miss a large drift that happens between dates.

Threshold rebalancing trades only when a weight moves outside a band around its target, such as ±5 percentage points on a 60% allocation. It responds to what the market did rather than to the date. The cost is that you have to monitor, and in a volatile year it can trigger several times.

Combined. Vanguard's analysis, covering 1926 to 2009 and updated since, found that checking on a schedule (annually or semi-annually) and trading only when a 5-point band was breached gave risk control close to monthly rebalancing with far fewer trades. That combination, check twice a year, act only outside the band, is the sensible default for a first portfolio.

Bands should scale with the allocation. A ±5-point band on a 60% holding is a relative move of about 8%. The same absolute band on a 5% satellite would let it double before triggering, so satellites get a relative band, typically ±25% of their target weight (a 7% target rebalances at 5.25% or 8.75%), or are governed by their stop and thesis review rather than by rebalancing at all.

The costs

Every rebalancing trade has three costs, and a plan that ignores them rebalances too often.

Transaction cost. Commissions are mostly zero for US-listed ETFs and stocks now, but the bid-ask spread is not. Broad ETFs like VTI and BND trade at spreads of a cent or two; thinly traded funds and small-cap stocks can cost 0.5% or more per round trip.

Tax, in a taxable account. Selling an appreciated holding realises a capital gain. Under IRS rules (Topic 409 and Publication 550), gains on lots held more than one year are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% depending on income; gains on lots held one year or less are taxed as ordinary income at your marginal rate, which for many people is 22% or 24%. In a tax-advantaged account such as an IRA or 401(k), rebalancing is free of this cost entirely, which is a reason to hold the more volatile parts of the allocation there if you have both types of account.

Time. Not a dollar cost, but the frequency of checking is also the frequency of temptation. Twice a year is enough.

Rebalancing without selling

Before selling anything in a taxable account, use the free levers:

  1. New contributions. Direct every new dollar to whichever asset is most underweight. With regular contributions, this alone keeps a portfolio near target most of the time.
  2. Dividends and interest. Turn off automatic reinvestment into the paying fund and direct the cash to the underweight asset instead.
  3. The cash reserve. The 5% T-bill sleeve from lesson 7 exists partly for this: it is the buffer you draw on to buy the underweight asset after a fall.
  4. Losses. If a holding is below its cost basis, selling it to rebalance realises a loss that offsets gains elsewhere, subject to the wash-sale rule (Publication 550: no repurchase of a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after).

Only when these are exhausted do you sell appreciated holdings, and when you do, sell the lots with the highest cost basis first and the lots older than a year in preference to newer ones.

Worked example

A 60/40 portfolio in a taxable account starts the year at $10,000: $6,000 in VTI, $4,000 in BND. Over the year VTI returns +25% and BND −5%.

End-of-year values.

  • VTI: 6,000 × 1.25 = $7,500
  • BND: 4,000 × 0.95 = $3,800
  • Total: $11,300
  • VTI weight: 7,500 ÷ 11,300 = 66.4%
  • BND weight: 3,800 ÷ 11,300 = 33.6%

The stock weight is 6.4 points over target, outside a 5-point band. Rebalance.

Target dollars.

  • VTI target: 0.60 × 11,300 = $6,780
  • BND target: 0.40 × 11,300 = $4,520
  • Sell VTI: 7,500 − 6,780 = $720
  • Buy BND: 4,520 − 3,800 = $720

Tax on the sale. The $720 of VTI sold was bought for 720 ÷ 1.25 = $576, so the realised gain is 720 − 576 = $144.

  • If the shares were held over a year and your long-term rate is 15%: tax = 144 × 0.15 = $21.60.
  • If held under a year and your marginal rate is 24%: tax = 144 × 0.24 = $34.56.

Alternative with no tax. Suppose you also planned to contribute $720 this year. Put the whole contribution into BND instead of splitting it:

  • VTI: $7,500 (unchanged)
  • BND: 3,800 + 720 = $4,520
  • Total: $12,020
  • VTI weight: 7,500 ÷ 12,020 = 62.4%

Not fully back to 60%, but inside the band, with no sale and no tax. The next contribution finishes the job.

Transaction cost. Selling $720 of VTI and buying $720 of BND at spreads of about 0.01% each costs roughly $0.14. Negligible for broad ETFs; the tax was the real cost, and it was avoidable.

Table

Calendar only Threshold only Calendar check + threshold act
Rule Trade to target on fixed dates Trade when a weight leaves its band Check on fixed dates; trade only if outside band
Monitoring effort Low High (continuous) Low
Trades per year (typical) 1 to 4, regardless of need 0 to several, depending on volatility 0 to 2
Risk control Good, with gaps between dates Tight Close to monthly rebalancing in Vanguard's tests
Tax and spread cost Can trade when drift is trivial Only when needed, but can cluster in volatile years Lowest of the three
Behavioural risk Low; the date decides Higher; you are watching constantly Low
Suited to Automated accounts, 401(k)s Experienced investors First portfolios in any account

The rule to write down

Check weights on two fixed dates a year. If any core holding is more than 5 points from target, or any satellite more than a quarter of its target away, restore it: first with contributions, dividends and the cash reserve; then, if still outside the band, by selling the highest-basis, longest-held lots of the overweight holding. Do nothing between the dates unless a satellite hits its stop. Lesson 12 puts this sentence into your investment plan.

Sources

  • Vanguard Research (Jaconetti, Kinniry, Zilbering), "Best practices for portfolio rebalancing", 2010: https://www.vanguard.com/pdf/icrpr.pdf
  • Internal Revenue Service, Topic No. 409, "Capital Gains and Losses": https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc409
  • Internal Revenue Service, Publication 550, "Investment Income and Expenses": https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550
  • U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov, "Rebalancing": https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/rebalancing
